questions.question: A healthy woman gives a pint of blood at a blood drive. Over the next several weeks, her body makes enough new red blood cells to replace all the ones she gave. Where in her body are the new red cells made?
questions.answer: In the marrow inside her bones
choices: In the marrow inside her bones
In the chambers of her heart
In the tissue of her liver
In the tissue of her spleen
questions.context: Red bone marrow, the soft tissue inside bones such as the hip bones, ribs and breastbone, makes the body's red cells, white cells and platelets. The heart pumps blood but makes none of it. The liver makes blood cells before birth and the spleen clears away worn-out red cells, but in a healthy adult the new cells come from the marrow.
questions.grade_note: Seventh-grade body-systems units teach that the skeletal system makes blood cells in the marrow, a job of the bones beyond support and protection.

questions.question: A newborn baby has somewhere near 300 bones, yet a grown adult has only 206. What happens to the extra bones as the child grows?
questions.answer: They join others to form single bones
choices: They join others to form single bones
They soften back into cartilage
They wear away as the others grow
They fall out, like baby teeth
questions.context: Many of a baby's bones start as separate pieces with cartilage between them, and as the child grows they harden and fuse. The plates of the skull close over the soft spots, five bones near the base of the spine fuse into one, the sacrum, and each hip bone forms from three. Cartilage turns into bone as a child grows, not the other way round.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade teaches the skeletal system and the adult count of 206 bones, and the baby's extra bones fusing is the usual reason given for that number.

questions.question: The biceps lies at the front of the upper arm, and the triceps at the back, and both work the elbow. A boy has his arm bent, and he straightens it to push open a heavy door. What do the two muscles do?
questions.answer: The triceps shortens and the biceps relaxes
choices: The triceps shortens and the biceps relaxes
The biceps shortens and the triceps relaxes
The biceps lengthens and pushes the arm straight
The triceps lengthens and pushes the arm straight
questions.context: A muscle can only pull, so the biceps and triceps work as a pair on opposite sides of the elbow. To straighten the arm, the triceps shortens and pulls while the biceps relaxes and is stretched out; to bend it again, the two swap jobs.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade teaches that skeletal muscles work in opposing pairs, with the biceps and triceps as the standard example.

questions.question: The lens of the eye focuses light into a sharp, upside-down picture on the retina, the thin lining at the back of the eye. The optic nerve links the eye to the brain. What travels from the eye to the brain along the optic nerve?
choices: A stream of electrical signals
A stream of the light itself
The upside-down picture, whole
The picture, turned right side up
questions.context: Light-sensing cells in the retina turn the light that falls on them into electrical signals, and the optic nerve carries those signals, not light or a picture, to the brain. The visual cortex, at the back of the brain, makes them into what a person sees.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade teaches that the sense organs send signals to the brain along nerves, and the eye is the usual example.

questions.question: A boy walking barefoot along a beach steps on a sharp shell. His foot jerks up at once, and a moment later he feels the sting. The jerk is a reflex. Where does the signal from his foot turn back as an order to the muscles of his leg?
choices: In his spinal cord
In his brain
In his leg muscles
In the skin of his foot
questions.context: In a reflex arc, a sensory nerve carries the signal to the spinal cord, which sends an order straight back along a motor nerve to the leg muscles, so the foot moves without waiting for the brain. The signal travels on up to the brain as well, which is why the sting is felt only after the foot has jerked away.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade teaches the reflex as a nervous-system response that runs through the spinal cord and skips the brain, which makes it faster.

questions.question: A rider is thrown from her horse, and the fall cuts right through her spinal cord in the middle of her back. Her legs themselves are not hurt at all, and the nerves in them are whole. What does she lose?
questions.answer: Feeling and movement below the injury
choices: Feeling and movement below the injury
Movement below the injury, but not feeling
Feeling below the injury, but not movement
Feeling and movement above the injury
questions.context: The spinal cord carries signals both ways, news from the senses up to the brain and the brain's orders down to the muscles. A cut through it stops both below the break, so she can neither feel nor move her legs, while everything above the break, her arms included, still works.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade teaches the brain, spinal cord and nerves as one system, with the spinal cord as the pathway for signals between the brain and the body.

questions.question: Robert Wadlow of Alton, Illinois, was still growing when he died in 1940, at 2.72 metres the tallest man on record. His pituitary, a gland the size of a pea at the base of his brain, made far too much growth hormone. How did the hormone reach the bones of his legs?
choices: It travelled in his blood
It ran down the nerves to his legs
It passed down his spinal cord
It soaked down through his skeleton
questions.context: Glands of the endocrine system release their hormones into the blood, which carries them to cells all over the body, so a gland in the head could lengthen bones in the legs. Nerves and the spinal cord carry electrical signals, not hormones. The pituitary is called the master gland, because its hormones also set other glands working.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade teaches that endocrine glands release hormones into the blood, and names the pituitary at the base of the brain as the gland that controls growth.

questions.question: A doctor finds that a woman's thyroid, a gland at the front of her neck, has begun making far too much of its hormone. Which sign would the doctor expect to see in her?
questions.answer: She loses weight though she eats more
choices: She loses weight though she eats more
She gains weight though she eats less
She feels cold even in a warm room
Her heart beats more slowly than before
questions.context: The thyroid's hormone sets how fast the body's cells burn the fuel from food, so too much of it burns food faster than she takes it in, and she also feels hot and has a racing heart. Too little does the opposite: weight gain, feeling cold and a slow heart.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade names the thyroid as the gland that controls how fast the body uses food for energy.

questions.question: Leonard Thompson, 13, lay dying of diabetes at Toronto General Hospital early in 1922, with far too much sugar in his blood. Doctors injected him with insulin, a hormone that the pancreas makes, purified from the pancreases of animals. Within a day his blood sugar fell sharply. How does insulin lower blood sugar?
questions.answer: It lets the body's cells take sugar in from the blood
choices: It lets the body's cells take sugar in from the blood
It breaks the sugar down while it is still in the blood
It stops the gut from taking in sugar from food
It sends the extra sugar out through the kidneys
questions.context: Insulin lets cells such as those of the muscles and liver take sugar out of the blood to use or store, so the level in the blood falls. In type 1 diabetes the body's own immune system destroys the cells of the pancreas that make insulin. Untreated diabetes does spill sugar into the urine, but because insulin is missing, not because insulin sends it there.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade teaches that the pancreas makes insulin and that too little of it causes diabetes; Thompson's injection in 1922 is the first story of insulin at work.

questions.question: A firework bangs behind a girl, and she jumps in a fraction of a second. Within moments her adrenal glands also release adrenaline into her blood. Minutes later, though she knows it was only a firework, her heart is still pounding. Why does the pounding outlast the jump?
questions.answer: The adrenaline keeps acting until her body clears it
choices: The adrenaline keeps acting until her body clears it
Her nerve signals take minutes to fade away
Her heart stores the adrenaline and lets it out slowly
The fright has strained her heart, and it must recover
questions.context: Nerve signals act in a fraction of a second, and their effect stops almost as soon as the signals do, but a hormone goes on working for as long as it stays in the blood. Adrenaline speeds the heart, sends extra sugar into the blood and slows digestion, and the body takes minutes to break it down. It is made in the adrenal glands, on top of the kidneys, not in the heart.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade names the adrenal glands and adrenaline in fright, and contrasts the nervous system's quick signals with slower, longer-lasting hormones.

questions.question: A barber trims a boy's hair and a nurse clips his fingernails, and neither hurts at all. Yet when his sister pulls out a single hair by the root, it stings. What are the trimmed hair and nails made of?
questions.answer: Dead cells packed with a tough protein
choices: Dead cells packed with a tough protein
Living cells that have no nerves
Hard minerals like those in bone
Dried oil from glands in the skin
questions.context: Hair and nails grow from living roots in the skin, but the parts that show are made of dead cells filled with keratin, a tough protein, so cutting them does not hurt. The root of a hair is wrapped in nerve endings, which is why pulling one stings. Nails are made of keratin like hair and the skin's outer layer, not of calcium like bone.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade teaches the integumentary system as the skin with its hair and nails, and that hair and nails are made of dead cells filled with keratin.
